parts.context: Two parents are discussing what to do after their son’s after-school program announces that it is closing.

lines: Theo, did you see the email from Maple Grove Kids Club? I read it twice because I thought I’d misunderstood it.
I saw the subject line on my phone, but I was in a meeting. What does it say?

They’re shutting down the after-school program at the end of this month. Apparently the church that rents them the basement has sold the building, and the new owners want the space empty by the thirtieth.
The end of this month? That gives us, what, three weeks? That’s outrageous. They must have known about the sale for ages and just didn’t bother telling the parents.

Well, to be fair, the director says the congregation only told her last Friday. She sounded pretty shaken in the email, actually. She’s offering a full refund for November, which is something, I guess.
A refund doesn’t pick Eli up at three fifteen, though. Your shift ends at five thirty, and I’m not off until six most days.

That’s the part that’s keeping me up at night. And it’s not just the pickup. He’s finally settled in there. Remember how he cried every morning in September? Now he talks about the chess club nonstop.
Yeah, changing everything again right before the holidays won’t be easy for him. Okay, so what are the options? I know my mother has offered to help before.
She has, but she lives in Stittsville. That’s a forty-minute drive each way, in winter, and she doesn’t love driving after dark anymore. I’d feel terrible asking her to do that five days a week.
Maybe not five days. But maybe she could cover a couple. Let’s keep her as a backup and see what else is out there first.

qs.q: Why is the after-school program closing?
o: The director has decided to retire at the end of the month.
The program is losing access to the place where it operates.
The congregation can no longer afford to support the program.
Too few families registered for the November session.
qs.ev: the new owners want the space empty by the thirtieth
qs.x: The building was sold and the new owners want the basement empty, so the program loses its space. The congregation is mentioned only as the group that informed the director, not as a funder.

qs.q: What is Rana’s attitude toward the program’s director?
o: She suspects the director kept the news from parents for weeks.
She is annoyed that the refund covers only one month.
She believes the director was also caught off guard.
She thinks the director should have found a new location.
qs.ev: the director says the congregation only told her last Friday
qs.x: Rana says “to be fair” and notes the director only learned last Friday and sounded shaken. The suspicion that the news was hidden is Theo’s view, not Rana’s.

qs.q: Why is Rana worried about moving Eli to a different program?
o: It took him a long time to feel comfortable at the current one.
He refuses to go anywhere without his chess club friends.
He has been crying every morning since September.
He would have to start in the middle of the holidays.
qs.ev: He’s finally settled in there
qs.x: “Finally settled in” means adjusting took a long time, so another change could be hard. The crying happened in September and has stopped, so option C uses the right words at the wrong time.

lines: What about the program at the Hillcrest Community Centre? It’s only ten minutes from his school.
I called them this morning. They have space, but only for kids who attend Hillcrest Elementary. Eli’s school isn’t on their walking route, and they won’t make exceptions.
Okay. What about a nanny share? The Okonkwos down the street were looking for another family to split a nanny with.

I thought about that, too. But they want someone full days for their toddler, so we’d be paying for eight hours to use three. Even split two ways, it would come to around nine hundred dollars a month. That’s triple what we pay now.
Triple? Yeah, that’s not happening. What if I talked to my manager about starting earlier? If I came in at seven, I could leave at three and get to the school by three thirty.
Could you, though? Last time you asked about flexible hours, she said the whole team had to be online for the morning meeting.
True, but that was before the reorganization. I’m on the client support side now, and half my colleagues start at seven anyway. I honestly think she’d say yes this time.
Then that’s worth asking. But three thirty is fifteen minutes after the bell. Who stays with him until you get there?
Doesn’t the school let kids wait in the library until three forty-five if a parent signs a form?
Right, Ms. Petrovic runs that. Okay, that could cover most days. But on Thursdays you have that standing call with the Vancouver office at four.

qs.q: Why can Eli not join the Hillcrest Community Centre program?
o: It has no spaces left for this school year.
It does not walk children from other schools.
It does not accept children partway through the year.
It only serves children enrolled at one particular school.
qs.ev: only for kids who attend Hillcrest Elementary
qs.x: The centre has space but takes only Hillcrest Elementary students and makes no exceptions. Option A is contradicted (“They have space”); the walking route is a consequence, not the rule itself.

qs.q: Why would the nanny share be so expensive for the family?
o: The nanny charges extra to look after two children.
They would have to cover the whole cost without another family.
They would be paying for a full day but only need part of it.
The nanny’s rates have tripled since last year.
qs.ev: we’d be paying for eight hours to use three
qs.x: They would pay for eight hours while needing only three, which makes it three times their current cost. “Triple” describes the comparison with their current fee, not a rise in the nanny’s rates.

qs.q: Why does Theo think his manager will now agree to his request?
o: His new role means an early start is already common.
His team has cancelled its morning meeting.
She agreed to flexible hours the last time he asked.
Several colleagues have requested the same schedule.
qs.ev: half my colleagues start at seven anyway
qs.x: After the reorganization he is in a group where many people already start at seven. Last time she refused, and nothing suggests the meeting was cancelled or that colleagues made requests.

lines: So Thursdays are a problem. And every second Friday, I’m on the late shift.
Which is where my mother comes in. One day a week, maybe two in a bad week. She said herself she’d love more time with him.
I suppose that could work. I just don’t want her on the highway in a snowstorm because we couldn’t get ourselves organized.
Then we tell her that if the roads are bad, she stays home and one of us leaves work early. No guilt.
Okay. And what about the library arrangement? Do we need to do anything?
You said Ms. Petrovic needs a signed form. Could you drop it off tomorrow? You go past the school on your way to your shift.
I can, but I’d rather email her tonight first to check there’s room. If thirty kids show up because Maple Grove closed, she might already have a waiting list.
Good point. Lots of families will be in the same boat. And I’ll talk to my manager first thing Monday. If she says no, we’re back to square one.
Let’s not say anything to Eli until we know for sure. He’ll have a hundred questions, and I want to have answers for him.
Agreed. Oh, and we prepaid December when we did the fall registration, so I’ll ask the club to refund that month as well, not just November.

qs.q: What does Rana mean when she says, “I suppose that could work”?
o: She is completely convinced by Theo’s plan.
She thinks Theo’s mother will probably refuse to help.
She would prefer to ask a different relative.
She accepts the idea but still has some doubts.
qs.ev: I suppose that could work
qs.x: “I suppose” signals reluctant agreement, and she immediately adds her worry about winter driving. She never suggests another relative or predicts a refusal.

qs.q: What will Rana do before dropping off the form?
o: Ask Theo’s mother to sign it for them
Wait until Theo has spoken to his manager
Contact the person in charge to see if there is space
Explain the new arrangement to Eli
qs.ev: I’d rather email her tonight first to check there’s room
qs.x: She will email Ms. Petrovic tonight to check there is room. Theo, not Rana, will speak to the manager, and they agree not to tell Eli yet.

parts.context: A parent is meeting with her daughter’s high school guidance counsellor.

lines: Thanks for seeing me on short notice, Mr. Adeyemi. Kata came home on Friday in tears and said she wants to drop chemistry. She’s never quit anything in her life, so I wanted to understand what’s going on before I sign anything.

I’m glad you came in. I met with Kata on Thursday. To be honest, her mark isn’t the disaster she thinks it is. She’s sitting at sixty-four, which is lower than she’s used to, but the first unit is always the hardest.
Sixty-four. She told me she was failing. Then again, she’s used to nineties.

That’s a big part of it, I think. Students who’ve always found school easy sometimes take their first sixty very personally. My concern is that if she drops chemistry now, it will close doors she may want open later. She mentioned nursing on her course selection form last year.
She did, and she still talks about it. Would dropping it really rule that out?

Most of the nursing programs in the province ask for Grade Twelve chemistry, and she can’t take that without this course. She could make it up in summer school, but the summer course runs four hours a day for five weeks, and it moves twice as fast. I wouldn’t recommend that route for a student who’s already anxious.
Then what do you suggest? I don’t want her miserable all year either.

The deadline to drop without it appearing on her transcript is October twenty-fourth, so she has about two weeks. In the meantime, there’s a peer tutoring program at lunch on Tuesdays and Thursdays, run by Grade Twelve students. And Ms. Barros, her chemistry teacher, offers extra help after school on Wednesdays.
Kata did mention Ms. Barros. I got the impression they don’t exactly get along.

I’ve heard that too, and frankly, I think it’s more about Kata feeling embarrassed to ask questions. So here’s my suggestion: she tries the peer tutoring for the next two weeks, and we meet again on the twenty-second, the three of us, before the deadline. If she’s still struggling then, we can talk about switching to a different science.
That sounds reasonable. I’ll need to sell it to her, though. She’s pretty set on dropping it.
Tell her it’s a two-week experiment, not a life sentence. That usually helps.

qs.q: Why did Mrs. Varga come to see the counsellor?
o: To sign the form that allows her daughter to drop a course
To learn more before agreeing to her daughter’s request
To complain about her daughter’s chemistry teacher
To ask about admission requirements for nursing
qs.ev: I wanted to understand what’s going on before I sign anything
qs.x: She wants to understand the situation before she signs, so she has not agreed yet. Nursing requirements come up later because the counsellor raises them, not because she came to ask.

qs.q: What does the counsellor suggest about Kata’s reaction to her mark?
o: She is unused to receiving average results.
She has misunderstood how the course is graded.
She is exaggerating so that she can drop the course.
She is failing because she missed the first unit.
qs.ev: Students who’ve always found school easy sometimes take their first sixty very personally
qs.x: He explains that a student used to nineties takes a mark in the sixties hard. He does not accuse her of exaggerating on purpose, and the first unit is described as difficult, not missed.

qs.q: Why does the counsellor not recommend summer school?
o: It does not count toward nursing admission.
It is only open to students entering Grade Twelve.
It costs more than taking the course during the year.
Its intensive pace could make Kata more stressed.
qs.ev: it moves twice as fast
qs.x: The summer course is long and fast, which he thinks is wrong for an anxious student. He actually says she could make up the course in summer school, so it does count.

qs.q: How does the counsellor view the tension between Kata and Ms. Barros?
o: He believes the teacher has been too strict with Kata.
He thinks Kata should ask to change classes.
He feels Kata’s self-consciousness is the real issue.
He suspects the teacher has marked Kata unfairly.
qs.ev: it’s more about Kata feeling embarrassed to ask questions
qs.x: He says the problem is “more about” Kata’s embarrassment than the teacher. He never criticizes Ms. Barros’s strictness or marking, and changing classes is not mentioned.

qs.q: What will most likely happen on October twenty-second?
o: Kata will begin the lunchtime peer tutoring.
Kata and her mother will review things with the counsellor.
Kata will hand in the form to drop chemistry.
The course will be removed from Kata’s transcript.
qs.ev: we meet again on the twenty-second, the three of us, before the deadline
qs.x: The twenty-second is the follow-up meeting with all three of them. Tutoring starts earlier, and the twenty-fourth (not the twenty-second) is the drop deadline.

parts.context: An incoming university student calls the residence office with questions about his housing offer.

lines: Hi, I’m an incoming first-year student, and I’ve been offered a room in Birchwood Hall. I have a few questions before I accept the offer.

Sure, and congratulations. Do you have your student number handy? Okay, Tomasz, I see the offer. You’ve been placed in a double room in Birchwood, which is our traditional-style building. You have until June fifteenth to accept and pay the deposit.
The deposit is five hundred dollars, right? Is that refundable if I change my mind?

It’s refundable, minus a seventy-five-dollar processing fee, up until July thirty-first. After that, it’s forfeited entirely. And just so you know, the deposit isn’t an extra charge. It gets applied to your winter-term fees.
Okay, good. Another thing. I was really hoping for a single room. Is there any way to switch?
Singles in Birchwood are very limited, and they go to upper-year students first. What I can do is add you to the waitlist. Realistically, though, most movement happens after the room freeze lifts.

For the first two weeks of September, no one can change rooms. It gives roommates a chance to settle in and lets us confirm who actually showed up. After that, if a single opens up, we contact people on the waitlist in the order they applied.
Got it. Now, the meal plan. My brother lived in residence and said it was really expensive. Do I have to buy one?

In Birchwood, yes. There are no kitchens, so everyone there must buy at least the basic plan, which is twenty-eight hundred dollars for the year. If you were in one of our suite-style buildings, like Larchmont, the plan would be optional, because the suites have their own kitchens.
Could I ask to be moved to Larchmont, then?
I’m afraid Larchmont is reserved for students in second year and up. Sorry.
Fair enough. One last thing. I play on the varsity volleyball team, and our training camp starts on August twenty-fifth. But move-in day is later than that, isn’t it?

Move-in for first-years is August thirty-first. But varsity athletes can arrive early. Your coach submits a list, and we bill the early nights to the athletics department rather than to you. So you don’t need to book anything yourself. Just make sure your coach has your name.
That’s a relief. I was about to ask how much early arrival costs.
For students who aren’t on that list, it’s forty dollars a night, but in your case it won’t apply.

qs.q: What happens to the deposit if Tomasz accepts the room and lives in residence?
o: It is returned to him in full at the end of the year.
It is counted toward an amount he will owe later.
It is reduced by a seventy-five-dollar processing fee.
It is kept by the university to cover any damage.
qs.ev: It gets applied to your winter-term fees
qs.x: The deposit is credited to his winter-term fees, so it is not an extra cost. The $75 fee applies only if he cancels before July 31.

qs.q: If Tomasz cancels in the middle of August, what will happen?
o: He will get $425 back.
He will get all $500 back.
He will lose the full $500.
He will be charged an extra $75.
qs.ev: After that, it’s forfeited entirely
qs.x: The partial refund ($500 − $75 = $425) is available only until July 31. Mid-August is after that date, so the whole deposit is lost.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the room freeze?
o: To give staff time to clean and inspect empty rooms
To make sure upper-year students receive singles first
To process waitlist requests in the order received
To let students adjust and the office check who has arrived
qs.ev: It gives roommates a chance to settle in and lets us confirm who actually showed up
qs.x: The freeze lets roommates adjust and allows the office to confirm attendance. The waitlist order applies after the freeze, and upper-year priority is a separate rule.

qs.q: Why must Birchwood residents buy a meal plan?
o: Their building has no cooking facilities.
All first-year students are required to have one.
The basic plan is cheaper than buying groceries.
Larchmont is full and cannot take more students.
qs.ev: There are no kitchens
qs.x: The plan is required in Birchwood because it has no kitchens. It is not required for all first-years: it is optional in suite-style buildings that have kitchens.

qs.q: Why can Tomasz not be moved to Larchmont?
o: It has no available suites until January.
Its meal plan costs more than Birchwood’s.
Its rooms are kept for varsity athletes.
It does not house students in their first year.
qs.ev: Larchmont is reserved for students in second year and up
qs.x: Larchmont is only for second-year students and above, and Tomasz is starting first year. Varsity athletes get early arrival, not special buildings.

qs.q: What does Tomasz need to do about arriving early for training camp?
o: Pay forty dollars for each night before move-in
Book his early nights directly through the residence office
Make sure he is included on a list sent by his coach
Ask the athletics department to pay him back later
qs.ev: Just make sure your coach has your name
qs.x: The coach sends a list and athletics is billed directly, so Tomasz only needs to be on the list. The forty-dollar rate is for students not on that list.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a new provincial program for adult learners.

lines: Workers over forty-five who want to retrain will soon be able to get help with the cost. The province announced today that it will launch the Mid-Career Skills Credit in January, covering eighty percent of tuition for short, job-focused college courses, up to a maximum of three thousand dollars per person. The program is open to people who are currently employed, as well as those who have lost their jobs in the past year. Courses must be at least thirty hours long and lead to a recognized certificate, which rules out most single-day workshops. The minister responsible said the credit is aimed at people whose jobs are being reshaped by automation, citing warehouse, manufacturing and administrative roles. A smaller pilot ran last year in three regions. Among the participants was Gerald Fontaine, a fifty-two-year-old shipping supervisor from Sudbury.

When they brought in the new inventory system at work, I’ll be honest, I was lost. The younger guys picked it up in a week. I took a six-week evening course in logistics software through the pilot, and it cost me about four hundred dollars out of pocket instead of two thousand. Without that, I probably would have just kept my head down and hoped nobody noticed. Now I’m the one training the new hires on the system.

Not everyone is applauding. The Provincial Federation of Labour says three thousand dollars won’t come close to covering longer programs, such as practical nursing or electrical apprenticeships, which can cost several times that amount. Colleges, meanwhile, are welcoming the funding but warn that evening and online sections fill quickly, and they may not be able to add instructors in time for the winter term. The province says it has set aside forty million dollars for the first year, which it estimates is enough for about sixteen thousand learners. Applications open January fifteenth through a new online portal. Employers who want to contribute toward the remaining twenty percent of tuition can register starting in March.

qs.q: Who is eligible for the new credit?
o: Only workers whose employers agree to pay part of the cost
Workers over forty-five, including some who are unemployed
Anyone who lost a job to automation in the last three years
Only people in warehouse, factory or office jobs
qs.ev: as well as those who have lost their jobs in the past year
qs.x: The credit is for workers over forty-five, whether employed or laid off within the past year. Warehouse and office jobs were only examples, and employer contributions are optional.

qs.q: Which course would NOT qualify for the credit?
o: A one-day workshop on spreadsheets
A forty-hour certificate in project management
A six-week certificate course in logistics software
A thirty-five-hour course with a recognized certificate
qs.ev: which rules out most single-day workshops
qs.x: Courses must be at least thirty hours and lead to a certificate, so a one-day workshop fails both tests. The other options meet the thirty-hour and certificate conditions.

qs.q: What does Gerald suggest about how he felt before taking the course?
o: His employer had ordered him to retrain.
He was already responsible for training all the new staff.
He had planned to change careers within a year.
He might have avoided facing the problem otherwise.
qs.ev: I probably would have just kept my head down and hoped nobody noticed
qs.x: Keeping his head down and hoping nobody noticed means he would have hidden his difficulty instead of dealing with it. Training new hires is what he does now, after the course.

qs.q: What concern do the colleges raise?
o: The credit is too small for longer programs.
The online portal may not be ready in time.
There may not be enough course spaces at first.
Older learners may struggle in online sections.
qs.ev: they may not be able to add instructors in time for the winter term
qs.x: Colleges worry that sections will fill and they cannot hire instructors quickly enough, meaning too few spaces. The complaint about longer programs comes from the labour federation.

qs.q: According to the report, how much would the province pay toward a qualifying course that costs $4,000?
qs.ev: up to a maximum of three thousand dollars per person
qs.x: Eighty percent of $4,000 is $3,200, but the credit is capped at $3,000, so the province pays $3,000. Option C forgets the maximum.

parts.context: Three members of an elementary school parent council are deciding how to spend a grant.

lines: Okay, let’s get started. As you know, the Larkspur Community Foundation approved our application for twelve thousand dollars for student well-being. We need to tell them by Friday how we plan to spend it. Sunita, you had a proposal?

I did. I think the obvious choice is the shade structure for the junior playground. Last June we had three kids sent home with heat exhaustion, and the quote we got from the installer was eleven thousand five hundred, so it fits almost perfectly.

I don’t disagree that the playground gets hot. But I keep coming back to the breakfast program. Right now it runs three days a week because we can’t afford food for five. Ms. Kowal told me the kids who come in hungry on Tuesdays and Thursdays are the same ones who end up in the office by ten.

I understand that, Brigitte, but the breakfast program is an ongoing cost. Twelve thousand would cover, what, two years of the extra days? Then we’re right back where we started. A shade structure lasts twenty years.

That’s a fair point about lasting value. But before we go further, there’s something in the foundation’s conditions I need to flag. The money has to be spent by June thirtieth next year. Any project on school property needs board approval, and Facilities told me that approval for permanent structures takes six to eight months, and that’s after we submit engineering drawings.
Six to eight months? We’re in November. Even if we submitted drawings in January, we’d be cutting it extremely close.
Closer than close. And if the money isn’t spent, it goes back to the foundation.
Well, that changes things. I wouldn’t want to risk losing the whole grant on a timeline we don’t control.
Not so fast. I still don’t love spending a one-time grant on something we’ll have to keep paying for. What happens in two years?

In two years we fundraise, like every other school. And honestly, by then we’ll have data showing the difference it makes. That’s a much easier case to make to donors than asking them to help us keep the lights on.

Can I suggest a middle path? The city has a matching program for school shade projects. They pay half, and the school community pays the other half. There’s no spending deadline, because it’s the city’s money on the city’s timeline. If we used part of this grant as our half...
Wait, the foundation money still has to be spent by June. If we hand it to the city as a matching contribution, does that count as spent?
I asked the foundation that exact question on Tuesday. They said yes, as long as the funds are transferred to the partner by June thirtieth, it counts.
So how would we split it?
The city’s quote for a smaller structure, covering just the sandbox area, is ten thousand. Our half is five. That leaves seven thousand for the breakfast program.
Seven thousand would cover the extra two days for about a year and a half. I could live with that.
A smaller structure is better than none, I suppose. And it buys us time to find longer-term breakfast funding. All right, I’m on board.
Then let’s vote. All in favour? Great, that’s unanimous. Sunita, could you draft the letter to the foundation? I’ll contact the city about the matching application.
I’ll have a draft to you by Wednesday.

qs.q: What reason does Sunita first give for choosing the shade structure?
o: It was the least expensive project available.
The installer had offered a discount to schools.
Children had already been affected by the heat.
The board had already approved the design.
qs.ev: Last June we had three kids sent home with heat exhaustion
qs.x: Three children were sent home with heat exhaustion, so the heat had already harmed students. The price “fits” the grant, but she never says it is the cheapest option or discounted.

qs.q: What does Brigitte imply about the students who arrive hungry?
o: They tend to have difficulties later in the morning.
They mostly attend school on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
They are sent to the program by Ms. Kowal.
They prefer to eat at home rather than at school.
qs.ev: the same ones who end up in the office by ten
qs.x: Ending up in the office by ten implies behaviour or health problems during the morning. Tuesdays and Thursdays are the days without breakfast, not the only days they attend.

qs.q: What is Sunita’s main objection to the breakfast program?
o: It does not help students who arrive late.
It already runs on all five school days.
Its food costs have doubled in two years.
It would need new money year after year.
qs.ev: the breakfast program is an ongoing cost
qs.x: She calls it an ongoing cost that the one-time grant would cover for only about two years. The program runs three days, not five, and no rise in food prices is mentioned.

qs.q: Why is the original shade plan risky?
o: The city would have to provide matching funds.
Approval might not arrive in time to spend the grant.
The installer’s price was expected to rise in January.
Engineering drawings would cost more than expected.
qs.ev: approval for permanent structures takes six to eight months
qs.x: With approval taking six to eight months after drawings, the June 30 spending deadline could be missed. January is when drawings might be submitted, not when a price rises.

qs.q: How does Sunita react when she hears about the deadline?
o: She insists the board could easily speed up its approval.
She suggests applying for a second grant instead.
She rethinks her position because of the uncertainty.
She accuses Wendell of hiding the conditions.
qs.ev: I wouldn’t want to risk losing the whole grant on a timeline we don’t control
qs.x: “That changes things” shows she reconsiders because the timeline is outside their control. She does not argue that approval could be faster or blame Wendell.

qs.q: Why does Brigitte believe fundraising will be easier in two years?
o: They will be able to show what the program has achieved.
Other schools will have stopped competing for the same donors.
The city will have finished paying for the shade.
Donors generally prefer paying for basic expenses.
qs.ev: by then we’ll have data showing the difference it makes
qs.x: Evidence of results will make a stronger case to donors. She actually says donors dislike requests to “keep the lights on”, the opposite of option D.

qs.q: What did the foundation tell Wendell?
o: The city cannot act as a partner on the project.
The deadline can be extended for building projects.
The grant may only be used for food or equipment.
Passing the money to a partner before the deadline is acceptable.
qs.ev: as long as the funds are transferred to the partner by June thirtieth, it counts
qs.x: The foundation counts money as spent if it is transferred to a partner by June 30. The deadline itself is not extended; it is the city’s own program that has no deadline.

qs.q: How much of the grant will go toward shade?
qs.ev: Our half is five
qs.x: The smaller structure costs $10,000 and the city pays half, so the council contributes $5,000. $7,000 is what remains for breakfasts; $11,500 was the original installer quote.

parts.context: You will hear a report about a proposal to end homework in elementary schools.

lines: When the Cedar Ridge School District proposed eliminating homework for students up to Grade Six, officials expected some debate. What they did not expect was eleven hundred written submissions in three weeks, more than for any proposal in the district’s history. Supporters of the ban point to research suggesting that, for young children, homework has little measurable effect on achievement. The one clear exception is reading. Children who read regularly at home tend to do better, which is why the proposal would still encourage twenty minutes of reading each night, though it would no longer be checked or graded. Supporters also argue that homework widens the gap between families. A child whose parent works evenings, or who doesn’t speak English at home, may get no help at all, while a classmate down the street has a parent, or a paid tutor, checking every answer. Under the current system, they say, homework often measures the home more than the child. But many teachers see it differently. Mireille Dufresne has taught Grade Four for nineteen years.

I’ll be the first to admit that a lot of homework is busywork, and I’ve assigned my share of it. But some things genuinely need practice that we don’t have time for in class. Multiplication facts are the best example. If a child doesn’t have them memorized by Grade Five, fractions become a nightmare. I’d rather fix homework than throw it out. Make it short, make it purposeful, and stop grading it.

Parents, too, are divided, and not always along the lines you might expect. Several parents who wrote in favour of the ban described evenings dominated by tears and arguments, and said they wanted their family time back. Yet a significant number of parents who work long hours opposed it, saying the homework folder is often the only way they know what their child is learning. One father wrote that without it, he would be parenting blind. Some families have suggested making homework optional instead. But Dufresne warns that this could reproduce the very inequality the ban is meant to address.
Who’s going to do the optional work? The kids whose parents are already sitting with them every night. The kids who most need the practice will be the ones who skip it.

The district’s trustees will vote on the proposal next month. Whatever they decide, several have already said the policy will be reviewed after a single school year, with input from teachers, families and, for the first time, students themselves. In the meantime, the district has asked schools to keep current homework practices in place, and several principals say they plan to hold information evenings so that parents can hear directly from teachers before the vote.

qs.q: What surprised district officials about the proposal?
o: How many parents supported the idea
How many teachers had stopped grading homework
How little research existed on the topic
How many people took the time to respond
qs.ev: What they did not expect was eleven hundred written submissions in three weeks
qs.x: The unexpected part was the record number of written submissions. Debate itself was expected, and parents turned out to be divided rather than mostly supportive.

qs.q: What would happen to nightly reading under the proposal?
o: It would be replaced by reading time in class.
Students would be urged to do it, but no one would monitor it.
It would be graded only for students in Grade Six.
Parents would be required to sign a reading log.
qs.ev: though it would no longer be checked or graded
qs.x: Reading would still be encouraged but no longer checked or graded, so it would not be monitored. Nothing is said about logs, class time or grading in Grade Six.

qs.q: What do supporters mean when they say homework “measures the home more than the child”?
o: Results depend heavily on how much help a child gets from family.
Teachers use homework to learn about students’ home lives.
Parents often end up completing the homework on their children’s behalf.
Homework is harder for children who live far from school.
qs.ev: homework often measures the home more than the child
qs.x: The phrase follows the example of children with or without help at home, so results reflect family support. Parents “checking” answers is mentioned, but not doing the work for the child.

qs.q: What is Ms. Dufresne’s position on homework?
o: It should be eliminated in every subject except reading.
It should be given only to students who are struggling.
It should be kept but redesigned to be brief and useful.
It should be graded so that students take it seriously.
qs.ev: I’d rather fix homework than throw it out
qs.x: She wants to keep homework but make it short and purposeful. She explicitly says to stop grading it, which rules out option D.

qs.q: Why did some parents who work long hours oppose the ban?
o: They had no time to help with homework at night.
They feared their children would spend more time watching television.
They wanted their children prepared for Grade Five.
Homework kept them informed about their child’s learning.
qs.ev: the homework folder is often the only way they know what their child is learning
qs.x: For these parents, the folder shows what their child is studying; without it they would be “parenting blind”. Grade Five was Dufresne’s example about multiplication, not the parents’ reason.

qs.q: What does Ms. Dufresne predict would happen if homework became optional?
o: Teachers would end up assigning more busywork.
Struggling students would be the least likely to complete it.
Parents would stop sitting with their children at night.
Students would be confused about what was expected.
qs.ev: The kids who most need the practice will be the ones who skip it
qs.x: She predicts that the students who need practice most would not do optional work, recreating inequality. Parents who already help would keep helping, not stop.

p1.meta: From: Odile Marchetti  |  To: Celeste Marchetti  |  Subject: Our new houseguest (and a small request)
p1.text:
Hi Celeste,

I can’t believe it’s already been three weeks since Haruto arrived! I promised I’d write once things settled down, and they finally have, mostly.

As you know, we signed up with the homestay agency in the spring, partly for the extra income and partly because Max and Lucie have been begging for an older “brother” ever since their cousins moved to Halifax. Haruto is sixteen and is spending the school year at Westdale Secondary. On paper, the arrangement is simple: we provide a room, meals and a “supportive family environment,” and the agency pays us a monthly allowance. In reality, it has been a bigger adjustment than I expected, for all of us.

The first week was awkward. Haruto was extremely polite but barely left his room, and I worried we’d done something wrong. It turned out he was exhausted and also convinced that he had to ask permission before opening the fridge. Once I gave him his own snack shelf, things improved almost overnight. Now he and Max shoot baskets in the driveway every evening, and he has even started teaching Lucie to make rice balls, with mixed results.

School is harder. His English is good, but he says the teachers speak quickly and he struggles to follow class discussions. His history teacher emailed me on Monday to say he hasn’t handed in two assignments. When I asked Haruto about it, he admitted he hadn’t understood the instructions and was too embarrassed to ask. I’ve arranged a meeting with the teacher next Thursday.

Which brings me to my favour. You spent all those years teaching English to adult newcomers, and I suspect you’d know exactly how to help him. Would you be willing to meet with him once a week, even by video, to go over his assignments? The agency gives us a small tutoring budget, forty dollars a week, so I’d insist on paying you.

Also, we’re planning to take him to the mountains over the long weekend in October. Would you and Graham like to join us? The cabin sleeps eight, so there’s plenty of room.

Let me know what you think. No pressure at all!

Love,
Odile

qs.q: Why did Odile’s family decide to host a student?
o: For financial reasons and because the children wanted an older sibling
Because the children’s cousins had recently moved to Halifax
Because Haruto’s parents are old friends of the family
Because Westdale Secondary asked local families to help
qs.ev: partly for the extra income and partly because Max and Lucie have been begging for an older “brother”
qs.x: Odile gives two reasons: extra income and her children’s wish for an older brother. The cousins’ move explains why the children wanted a “brother”, but it is not the family’s reason for hosting.

qs.q: What does Odile suggest about the agency’s description of hosting?
o: It was deliberately misleading about the payments.
It did not mention that students might need tutoring.
It made hosting sound simpler than it has turned out to be.
It required more meals than the family could provide.
qs.ev: On paper, the arrangement is simple
qs.x: “On paper … simple” followed by “In reality … a bigger adjustment” contrasts the description with the experience. She does not accuse the agency of lying, and it does provide a tutoring budget.

qs.q: What explains Haruto’s behaviour during his first week?
o: He was homesick and missed his own family.
He was tired and unsure of the household rules.
He felt uncomfortable around Max and Lucie.
He disliked the meals that Odile was preparing for him.
qs.ev: It turned out he was exhausted and also convinced that he had to ask permission before opening the fridge
qs.x: He was exhausted and thought he needed permission to use the fridge, so he was tired and unsure of the rules. Homesickness is never mentioned, and he now plays happily with Max.

qs.q: In the letter, what does “with mixed results” suggest about the cooking lessons?
o: Lucie has learned to make rice balls perfectly.
Haruto has decided to stop teaching Lucie.
The whole family now cooks dinner together each evening.
Lucie’s attempts have been only partly successful.
qs.ev: with mixed results
qs.x: “Mixed results” means some attempts work and some do not. It does not mean the lessons stopped, and Lucie has clearly not mastered the skill yet.

qs.q: Why did Haruto fail to hand in his history assignments?
o: He was unclear about the task and too shy to seek help.
His history teacher speaks too quickly in class.
He was spending his evenings playing basketball.
He had been given the wrong deadline by the agency.
qs.ev: he admitted he hadn’t understood the instructions and was too embarrassed to ask
qs.x: He did not understand the instructions and was too embarrassed to ask. Fast-speaking teachers explain why discussions are hard, but Haruto gives a different reason for the missing work.

qs.q: What is Odile’s main request to Celeste?
o: To attend the meeting with the history teacher
To find a qualified English tutor for Haruto
To help Haruto with his schoolwork on a regular basis
To lend the family a cabin for the long weekend
qs.ev: Would you be willing to meet with him once a week
qs.x: The favour is weekly sessions to go over assignments. Odile will attend the teacher meeting herself, and the cabin is already Odile’s plan; Celeste is only invited.

reply.intro: Here is Celeste’s response to Odile. Complete the response by choosing the best option for each blank.
reply.text:
Dear Odile,

What a lovely update! I laughed out loud at the image of Haruto {1}. Poor kid. I remember feeling exactly the same way with my host family in Lyon when I was his age.

Of course I’ll help, and I’d be happy to do it for free. Please put the agency’s money toward {2} instead. From what you describe, his problem isn’t really his English. Students from very formal school systems often believe that {3}, so we’ll practise polite ways of asking a teacher for clarification. I’d also suggest that before you meet his history teacher, you {4}, so that he doesn’t feel he’s being talked about behind his back.

As for October, I’d love to come, but Graham {5}. I’ll ask him tonight and let you know by the weekend.

Hugs to everyone,
Celeste

o: teaching Lucie to shoot baskets
waiting for permission to open the fridge
refusing to come out of the cabin
writing emails to his history teacher
blanks.ev: convinced that he had to ask permission before opening the fridge
blanks.x: The funny image from the letter is Haruto thinking he needed permission to open the fridge. Basketball was with Max, and Lucie was learning to cook, not to shoot baskets.

o: the cabin rental for the long weekend
school supplies for Max and Lucie
a second snack shelf for the kitchen
something fun for Haruto, like a sports club
blanks.ev: The agency gives us a small tutoring budget
blanks.x: The budget is meant for Haruto, so if Celeste works for free it should still benefit him. The cabin and the other children’s supplies are not what the agency money is for.

o: asking questions in class is rude or risky
Canadian teachers speak too fast to follow
assignments should always be handed in early
group work is more useful than lectures
blanks.x: Celeste links his silence to a belief about asking questions, which fits “too embarrassed to ask” and her plan to practise asking for clarification. Fast speech was mentioned but does not explain the planned practice.

o: cancel it and simply email the teacher instead
let the agency deal with the problem
ask Haruto whether he would like to come
send Haruto to meet the teacher alone
blanks.ev: so that he doesn’t feel he’s being talked about behind his back
blanks.x: Inviting Haruto to the meeting means he would not feel discussed behind his back. Sending him alone would contradict Odile’s plan to attend herself.

o: might have promised to help his brother move then
has already said he would love to join you
has never actually met Max and Lucie
has already booked the cabin for all of us
blanks.ev: I’ll ask him tonight and let you know

p3.title: Back to the Workshop: Why Shop Class Is Making a Comeback
paras: For much of the twentieth century, nearly every Canadian high school had a woodworking or auto shop. By the early 2000s, many of those rooms had been converted into computer labs or storage space. Budget pressures played a role, since equipment is expensive to maintain and insurance costs rose sharply after several well-publicized injuries, but so did a cultural shift. Guidance counsellors, under pressure to raise university acceptance rates, often steered strong students away from technical electives, which came to be seen as a fallback for those who were “not academic.” Enrolment fell, and when experienced shop teachers retired, schools frequently chose not to replace them. In some districts, the only remaining technical courses were offered at a single specialized school, which meant a long bus ride for any student who wanted to take them.

The tide began to turn as employers in construction, manufacturing and the automotive sector warned of a looming shortage of skilled workers. With a large share of tradespeople approaching retirement, several provinces introduced funding to reopen and re-equip school workshops. Programs that allow students to earn hours toward an apprenticeship while still in high school have expanded quickly; in one province, participation more than doubled over five years. Teachers report that the students signing up today look different, too. “Ten years ago, it was mostly kids who were struggling in their other classes,” said one technology teacher in Saskatoon. “Now I’ve got students who are also taking calculus and physics, and they want to know how to actually build what they design.” Some schools now have waiting lists for courses they could barely fill a decade ago.

Advocates argue that the benefits of hands-on learning extend well beyond preparing future electricians and carpenters. Measuring, cutting and assembling a project requires students to apply geometry in a way that a worksheet rarely does, and mistakes have immediate, visible consequences. Several teachers interviewed for this article said that students who are disengaged in conventional classes often show unexpected persistence in the shop, staying after the bell to fix an error rather than abandoning the work. There is also evidence that practical courses improve attendance. A study of one urban school board found that students enrolled in at least one technical elective were noticeably less likely to miss school than similar students who were not, although the researchers cautioned that more motivated students may simply be more likely to choose such courses.

Despite the renewed interest, serious obstacles remain. The most pressing is staffing. A qualified technology teacher typically needs both trade experience and a teaching degree, and a skilled electrician can often earn considerably more on a job site than in a classroom. Some boards have responded by creating accelerated teacher-education programs for experienced tradespeople, but these remain small. Equipment is another hurdle: a modern shop may require computer-controlled routers and 3D printers alongside traditional tools, and grants rarely cover ongoing maintenance. Finally, attitudes are slow to change. Many parents still see a university degree as the only respectable route, and some students admit they hesitate to sign up for a shop course because of how it might look on their transcript to admissions officers.

qs.q: Students who wanted technical courses sometimes had to travel to another school.
qs.ev: which meant a long bus ride for any student who wanted to take them
qs.x: Paragraph A: in some districts, technical courses existed at only one school, requiring a long bus ride.

qs.q: The profile of students choosing technical courses has shifted.
qs.ev: Teachers report that the students signing up today look different, too.
qs.x: Paragraph B: the teacher now sees students who also take calculus and physics, not only struggling students.

qs.q: Hands-on projects turn mathematical ideas into something concrete.
qs.ev: requires students to apply geometry in a way that a worksheet rarely does
qs.x: Paragraph C: building a project forces students to apply geometry, unlike a worksheet.

qs.q: Better pay elsewhere can make it hard to attract tradespeople into teaching.
qs.ev: a skilled electrician can often earn considerably more on a job site than in a classroom
qs.x: Paragraph D: staffing is the biggest obstacle because tradespeople earn more on job sites.

qs.q: Injuries in school workshops have declined since safety rules were updated.
qs.x: Paragraph A mentions injuries that raised insurance costs, but nothing is said about updated rules or a decline in injuries.

qs.q: The connection between technical courses and attendance may not be caused by the courses themselves.
qs.ev: the researchers cautioned that more motivated students may simply be more likely to choose such courses
qs.x: Paragraph C: researchers warn that motivated students may choose these courses, so the courses may not cause the better attendance.

qs.q: Accelerated teaching programs for tradespeople receive more applications than they can accept.
qs.x: Paragraph D says these programs “remain small”, but it says nothing about the number of applicants or waiting lists.

qs.q: High school apprenticeship programs are more popular in Saskatchewan than in any other province.
qs.x: Paragraph B mentions a teacher in Saskatoon and growth in “one province”, but never compares Saskatchewan with other provinces.

qs.q: Some students fear that a technical course could weaken their university applications.
qs.ev: because of how it might look on their transcript to admissions officers
qs.x: Paragraph D: some students hesitate because of how a shop course might look to admissions officers.

p4.title: Letter Grades Belong in the Past
p4.byline: Opinion | by Harriet Osei-Bonsu, retired elementary school principal
p4.text:
Every June, parents across Canada open an envelope, or, more often now, a school portal, and scan their child’s report card for one thing: the letters. A B+ in science sparks a celebration; a C in reading sets off a week of anxiety. I spent thirty-one years in elementary schools, the last twelve as a principal, and I have come to believe that those letters do more harm than good for children under twelve.

My objection is not that grades are harsh. It is that they are vague. A B in mathematics tells a parent almost nothing about what a nine-year-old can actually do. Has she mastered multiplication but struggled with measurement? Did she start the term well below grade level and make remarkable progress, or did she coast? A single letter averages all of this into a blur. Worse, it averages behaviour into achievement. In my experience, many teachers quietly lower marks for late work or messy notebooks, which means two children with identical understanding can come home with different grades.

There is also the question of what grades do to young learners’ motivation. Children quickly learn to ask, “Is this for marks?” and to invest effort accordingly. Students who receive low grades early often conclude that they are simply “bad at math,” a belief that can follow them for years. Students who receive high grades, meanwhile, may become reluctant to attempt anything difficult in case they spoil their record.

What should replace letter grades? Several school boards have already moved to standards-based reporting, in which each subject is broken into specific skills, such as reading comprehension, fluency and written expression, and each skill is rated on a four-level scale, from “beginning” to “extending.” Every rating is paired with a short comment explaining what the child can do and what comes next. Behaviour and work habits are reported separately, so they no longer distort the academic picture.

I am well aware of the objections. Parents tell me they find letter grades easy to understand, and they worry that a four-point scale is simply a letter grade in disguise. That concern is fair, but it is a reason to explain the new system carefully, not a reason to keep the old one. When my own school piloted standards-based reports, we held evening sessions for families and translated our guides into six languages. By the second year, complaints had fallen to a handful.

The more serious objection is workload. Writing meaningful comments for twenty-eight students across a dozen skills takes time, and teachers are already stretched. I will not pretend otherwise. But boards that are serious about this change must pay for it, through release days for report writing and shared comment banks that teachers can adapt rather than invent from scratch. A reform that relies on teachers’ unpaid evenings will not last.

Some critics argue that children must eventually get used to grades, since high schools and universities use them. But we do not teach six-year-olds to drive because they will need a licence at sixteen. Readiness matters. By Grade Seven or Eight, students are far better able to understand a grade as a measure of one piece of work rather than as a verdict on who they are.

Letter grades are a habit, not a law of nature. For our youngest learners, we can do better.

qs.q: What is the writer’s main criticism of letter grades?
o: They are too harsh on students who struggle.
They hide important details about a child’s abilities.
They are calculated differently by every school board.
They encourage parents to compare their children.
qs.ev: It is that they are vague.
qs.x: Her objection is vagueness: one letter blurs what a child can and cannot do. She explicitly says her objection is “not that grades are harsh”.

qs.q: According to the writer, why might two students with the same understanding receive different grades?
o: One of them made more progress during the term.
Their teachers used completely different four-level scales.
One of them had mastered multiplication earlier.
Their marks may also reflect habits like lateness.
qs.ev: many teachers quietly lower marks for late work or messy notebooks
qs.x: Teachers lower marks for late or messy work, so behaviour changes the grade. Progress during the term is something a letter hides, not a reason for different grades.

qs.q: How does the writer respond to parents who say letter grades are easy to understand?
o: She accepts the concern but says it calls for better explanation.
She argues that parents should not focus on report cards.
She suggests keeping letters alongside the new scale.
She claims that most parents’ complaints are exaggerated.
qs.ev: it is a reason to explain the new system carefully, not a reason to keep the old one
qs.x: She calls the concern fair and answers it with family sessions and translated guides. She never proposes keeping both systems or dismisses parents as exaggerating.

qs.q: What does the writer imply about reforms that depend on teachers working extra hours for free?
o: They are the quickest way to introduce change.
They are acceptable during a pilot year.
They are unlikely to survive in the long run.
They should be paid for by parent councils.
qs.ev: A reform that relies on teachers’ unpaid evenings will not last.
qs.x: She says such a reform “will not last”, so boards must fund release days. Her pilot is mentioned in another paragraph and has nothing to do with unpaid work.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention teaching six-year-olds to drive?
o: To show that young children learn practical skills quickly
To argue that some things should wait until children are ready
To suggest that grades can be as dangerous as cars
To compare report cards with driving tests
qs.ev: Readiness matters.
qs.x: The comparison answers critics who say children must get used to grades early: we wait for readiness. It is not about danger or about tests.

t1.situation: You have applied to a college diploma program in early childhood education. Two days before the application deadline, you receive a message saying that your high school transcript has not been received, although your former school says it sent the transcript three weeks ago.
bullets: Explain the situation and what you have done so far

t1.model:

t2.intro: Your local school board is considering changes to the school calendar for elementary and secondary students and has asked families and community members for their opinion. The total number of school days will stay the same.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: A balanced calendar: summer break is shortened to six weeks, and students get three two-week breaks during the year (in November, February and April).
t2.b: The traditional calendar with small changes: summer break stays at about nine weeks, winter break is extended to two and a half weeks, and a one-week break is added in early November.
t2.model:
Although I understand the appeal of a balanced calendar, I prefer Option B, the traditional calendar with small changes.

My main reason is that the long summer break still matters to many families and students. Teenagers rely on summer jobs to save for college, and those jobs usually require eight or nine weeks of availability. Many children also attend camps or spend time with grandparents who live far away, which is much harder to arrange in a six-week window.

I also think Option B solves the biggest problem with the current calendar. The fall term is long and exhausting, and teachers often say that students are burned out by November. Adding a week off in early November and extending the winter break would give everyone a real chance to rest.

Supporters of the balanced calendar argue that shorter summers reduce learning loss, and that is a fair point. However, three two-week breaks would create serious child care problems for working parents, who would need to find coverage six extra weeks a year.

Overall, Option B improves the calendar without disrupting family life.

t1.prompt: Your friend’s eighteen-year-old son has been accepted into a university engineering program, but he wants to take a gap year to work and travel first. Your friend is worried that he will never go back to school. Advise your friend about how to handle the situation.
t1.model: I completely understand why you’re nervous, but honestly, a gap year can be a great thing if it’s planned properly. The first thing I’d do is find out whether the university will let him defer his acceptance. A lot of programs allow students to hold their spot for a year, and if he has a guaranteed place waiting for him, the risk of him never going back is much smaller. Second, I’d sit down with him and ask him to put his plan on paper. What kind of work is he looking for, how much does he want to save, and where does he want to travel? If he can’t answer those questions, it’s a sign he needs more time to think it through. On the other hand, if he has a clear plan, you might be impressed. I’d also suggest that he work for at least part of the year in something related to engineering, like a construction site or a machine shop. That way, he’ll come back with real experience and probably more motivation. Finally, try not to turn this into a fight. If he feels you trust him, he’s much more likely to keep his promise and start school next fall.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when a teacher, coach or mentor changed the way you thought about something. What happened, and how did it affect you?
t2.model: When I was in Grade Ten, I was convinced I was terrible at writing. I always got my essays back covered in red ink, so I just stopped trying. Then I had an English teacher named Mr. Okafor, who did something nobody had done before. Instead of marking my first essay, he asked me to stay after class and tell him what I was trying to say. I explained my argument out loud, and he said, “That’s brilliant. Now write exactly what you just told me.” It sounds simple, but it completely changed how I saw writing. I realized I didn’t have a thinking problem; I had a confidence problem. By the end of that year, my marks had gone up by almost twenty percent. Even now, whenever I’m stuck on a report at work, I explain it out loud first.

scene.alt: A busy school classroom during a science fair. A whiteboard at the top says SCIENCE FAIR, and a clock and a window are on the wall. On the left, a girl in a green shirt points at an orange box labelled SOLAR OVEN on a wooden table, next to a small plant. In the centre, a teacher with glasses and a grey bun holds a book or clipboard and listens to her. On the right, a boy in a red shirt stands beside a second table with a laptop and holds a blue balloon. A father in a blue shirt takes a photo, and a woman in a purple dress holds a cup.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This looks like a science fair in a school classroom. At the top of the picture there’s a whiteboard that says “Science Fair,” and there’s a clock and a window on the wall. On the left, a girl in a green shirt is standing next to a wooden table, pointing proudly at an orange box labelled “Solar Oven.” Right beside her, a teacher with glasses and grey hair in a bun is holding what looks like a clipboard, so she’s probably judging the projects. On the right side, a boy in a red T-shirt is standing beside another table with a laptop on it, and he’s holding a blue balloon, maybe as part of his experiment. A dad in a blue shirt is taking a photo, and a woman in a purple dress is holding a coffee and looking around. It feels lively and a little nervous.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the teacher will finish listening to the girl with the solar oven and write some notes on her clipboard. Then she’ll probably ask the girl to show how the oven actually works, so the girl might open the box and take out something she cooked, like a melted marshmallow. After that, the teacher will move on to the boy in the red shirt. He looks a bit nervous, and since he’s holding a balloon, I imagine his project is about air pressure. He might try to demonstrate it, and there’s a good chance the balloon will pop by accident, which would make everyone jump and then laugh. The dad with the camera will definitely take a picture of that moment. Later, I expect all the students will gather at the front by the whiteboard, and the teacher will announce the winners of the science fair.

t5.intro: Your family is choosing a summer day camp for your nine-year-old son. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Coding & Robotics Camp
details: Kids build and program a robot

t5.persuade: Your partner prefers the overnight sports camp. Persuade your partner that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know the sports camp looks exciting, and I agree he’d love the swimming. But I really think the Wilderness Explorers camp is a better fit this year. First, look at the cost. The overnight camp is nine hundred and fifty dollars for a single week, while Wilderness Explorers is only two hundred and eighty. For the same money, he could go for three weeks. Second, he’s only nine, and he’s never slept away from home. Last time he stayed at your sister’s, he called us at midnight. A three-hour drive away, we couldn’t just go and get him. With the day camp, he gets adventure, but he’s home every night. And honestly, he plays soccer and basketball all year already. Canoeing and fire safety would teach him something new. Let’s save the overnight camp for when he’s eleven.

t6.situation: Your younger brother is applying for a university scholarship and asked you to read his essay. You notice that a large part of it is almost identical to an essay you found online. The deadline is tomorrow at noon, and he has already told your parents the essay is finished.
options: Talk to your brother and explain why he must rewrite the essay.
Talk to your parents and explain why you are worried about the essay.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey, Sami, can I talk to you about your essay for a minute? First, I want to say the ideas in it are good, and I can tell you really want this scholarship. But I found a sample essay online, and some of your paragraphs are almost word for word the same. I’m not saying you did it on purpose, but scholarship committees use software that checks for this, and if they find it, you won’t just lose this scholarship. It could follow you to university. I know the deadline is tomorrow at noon, but there’s still time. Let’s sit down tonight after dinner. You talk me through why you want to study biology, and I’ll help you organize it into your own words. I don’t need to tell Mom and Dad anything. I just want you to submit something you’re proud of.

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should college and university tuition be free for all students in Canada? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, tuition should not be completely free for everyone, but it should be free or close to free for students from low- and middle-income families. Let me explain why. First, education is one of the best investments a country can make. When more young people can study, the economy gains skilled workers, and those graduates pay more in taxes over their lifetimes. Right now, many talented students choose not to apply, or they drop out, because they’re afraid of debt. A friend of mine left nursing school after one year because she couldn’t afford rent and tuition at the same time, even though we desperately need nurses. On the other hand, making tuition free for every student, including those from wealthy families, would cost billions of dollars. That money would have to come from somewhere, possibly from health care or from schools. Families who can easily afford tuition don’t need a subsidy. So I think the fairest approach is to use income to decide. Students from families below a certain income should pay nothing, and others should pay on a sliding scale. That way, cost is never the reason a capable student gives up on their education, but public money is spent where it makes the biggest difference.

scene.alt: An unusual classroom where an enormous, friendly golden dog, about as tall as the whiteboard, is lying calmly in the middle of the room. Three children are sitting on the floor leaning against the giant dog, each reading a book. A teacher in a yellow dress stands on the left beside a bookshelf, smiling and holding a book. A whiteboard at the back says READ TO ROSIE. There is a window, a clock and a plant in the corner.

t8.prompt: Your sister is choosing a school for her seven-year-old son, who is very nervous about reading aloud. You visited this school’s open house and saw this classroom. Call your sister, describe what you saw, and explain whether you think she should consider this school. Your sister cannot see the picture.
t8.model: You won’t believe what I saw at the Elmview open house. In one classroom, there was a dog lying in the middle of the floor, but it was enormous, about as tall as the whiteboard. It was golden and fluffy and completely calm, with its eyes half closed. Three kids were sitting on the floor, leaning against it like a giant cushion, and each of them was reading a book to it. The whiteboard said “Read to Rosie,” so I guess that’s the dog’s name. The teacher was standing by the bookshelf, smiling. Honestly, I think you should consider this school for Leo. He gets so anxious reading in front of other kids, but a dog doesn’t judge anyone. My only worry is his allergy, so you’d need to ask whether Rosie sheds.
